stories.title: Trump predicts deal with Russia on Ukraine and Europe
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has predicted an imminent deal with Russia covering Ukraine and "all of Europe", after his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, hosted officials from the two warring countries at the White House. Mr Trump revealed he had an unscheduled meeting with Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy, following his involvement in the event hosted by the US first lady. Mr Trump's comments will fuel Ukrainian and European fears that he is pivoting towards the Kremlin for a larger deal that could reduce the US military presence on the continent and give Moscow more sway. They also come the week before three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to resume in Abu Dhabi, capital of the UAE, for the first time since February. While Ms Trump called for an "enduring" Ukraine ceasefire to follow up the brief truce she brokered in a Russian-occupied town, her 80-year-old husband indicated that an unspecified "very big" deal was close. "I can't tell you what I discussed. But I'm just telling you, it's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement," Mr Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked about his talks with Mr Dmitriev.

stories.title: Aer Lingus nine month operating profits drop by 57%
stories.summary: Aer Lingus has reported an operating profit of €142m for the third quarter of 2026, down €28m from the €170m recorded the same time last year on the back of increased fuel costs and a changed competitive environment across its operations. The airline, which is owned by IAG, said its operating profit for the nine months to the end of Septmber slumped by 57% to €108m from €250m in the same period in 2025. Aer Lingus said its passenger numbers increased by 1.8% in the three months from July to September, but added that competitive market conditions and a weaker yield environment have limited its ability to offset higher fuel and other operating costs. Aer Lingus said its financial performance so far this year reflects the continuing structural challenges in its operating environment. "This includes a fundamentally changed competitive environment following increased competitor capacity in recent years, particularly across the North Atlantic," it stated. "Aer Lingus has also experienced higher supplier and carbon costs and significantly increased fuel costs. These structural challenges are expected to continue through the airline's upcoming seasonally weaker quarters and through 2027," it added.

stories.title: O'Donoghue: Limerick back on top with aggressive pursuit
stories.summary: An aggression in the way they went about things was the driving force for Limerick as they scaled the hurling summit again in 2026, according to Will O'Donoghue. The Shannonsiders ended a wait of three years for national silverware, claiming the Division 1 and All-Ireland titles in fine style. For a county that had hoovered up the majority of the prizes since 2018, a three-year gap no doubt felt like an eternity. O'Donoghue's efforts at centre-back were rewarded with a third All-Star. Further recognition in being named the Gaelic Writers' Association Hurling Personality of the Year saw him reflect on the year, a campaign where the Treaty camp savoured the sweet smell of success again. "It's huge satisfaction because whether anyone wants to admit it or not you do start questioning if you will get back there", said O'Donoghue. "When you're winning, you think that'll be the case forever. So I mean to get back there, achieve what we wanted, (and) win the three major trophies this year, was obviously a huge, huge amount of satisfaction in that. "Even if you take the Tipperary game this year in the [Munster] round-robin, I mean there's huge satisfaction, while there may have been a larger score difference between let's say that and the Clare game in the semi-final, you're still getting huge satisfaction in winning a game in the Gaelic Grounds, in winning a Munster championship match, and delivering a good performance like that. I think we were just very keen to put in good performances and win as many games as we could.

stories.title: Beyond AI: Beta Festival reimagines our relationship with nature
stories.summary: Beta Festival Creative Producer Sophie Delaney introduces this year's edition of the Beta Festival, the Dublin-based event which explores how technology can change the way we understand the world beyond ourselves. I had followed Beta Festival and the work of Irish digital artists and researchers from my home in Australia, so moving to Ireland last year felt like an opportunity to get to know a scene I had long admired from afar. Beta’s Director, Aisling Murray, took a chance on an Aussie she had only met over Zoom, and we quickly bonded over our shared love of art and technology (and occasional fear of both). Now in its fourth edition, Beta Festival (founded by Aisling Murray and The Digital Hub), has grown from an annual festival into a year-round platform for art, technology and society. This year, the festival asks what happens when we move beyond a human-centred perspective and consider the intelligence of landscapes, plants, animals and machines. At a time when so much attention is focused on artificial intelligence, the programme invites us to think more broadly about how technology shapes our relationships with the living world. Across Dublin, the festival presents 14 new artworks by Irish and international artists, spanning installation, performance, sound, and interactive digital media as well as the Irish premiere of existing works from internationally renowned performers. What excites me is how differently these artists approach these questions, often finding unexpected ways to make complex ideas accessible. SEED: Signal and Trace, is a Coalesce research project led by Trish Morgan and István László, bringing together six new commissions exploring environmental change through sensory experiences of data. Wind, carbon dioxide and temperature readings become material for artworks that we can experience through sound, scent, touch and sight. Meanwhile, Unmasking Nature, led by AlanJames Burns, invites visitors into a multisensory environment inspired by Ireland’s biodiversity, exploring the connections between neurodiversity and the natural world. At a time when so much attention is focused on artificial intelligence, the programme invites us to think more broadly about how technology shapes our relationships with the living world. We are also presenting new commissions from Cezar Mocan and Hung Lu Chan through Studiotopia, our European project bringing artists and scientists together. As well as commissions through our Local Artists Network (showcasing Irish-based practitioners) including Serena Devereux, whose interactive work draws on real-time weather data, and 1iing Heaney, who explores ecology and the Irish landscape.

stories.summary: Carlow actress Ella Lily Hyland has spoken about the importance of hearing her native accent on screen, saying it is "incredibly special" to represent where she comes from. Carlow actress Ella Lily Hyland has praised the makers of Netflix spy thriller Black Doves for allowing her to perform in her native accent. The 28-year-old plays assassin Williams in the hit series, which returned for a second season this week. She stars alongside Welsh actress Gabrielle Creevy, who plays fellow assassin Eleanor, and Keira Knightley, who portrays Helen Webb, a spy working for the shadowy Black Doves organisation. Speaking to the Press Association, Hyland said being able to use her own accent was particularly meaningful. "Growing up not seeing your own accent represented on screen, and then having the opportunity to do that yourself, is incredibly special," she said.

stories.title: Met Gala update 2027 theme following Galliano backlash
stories.summary: Earlier today, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that its 2027 Costume Institute exhibition and Met Gala will now take place under the theme: "extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday". Asking guests "to see the everyday anew," the red-carpet event and accompanying exhibition will focus on commonplace materials made remarkable through design. The Met Gala had previously planned to honour controversial designer John Galliano in 2027, but the theme was dropped in August 2026, when the designer walked away amid mounting backlash over his past racist and antisemitic comments. Speaking at the time, he stated: "After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time". Organised by Andrew Bolton, Curator in Charge of the Costume Institute in New York City, 'John Galliano: Horizons' was due to open on 3 May and celebrate Galliano's work and influence on the fashion industry across four decades. Organisers say they had planned to examine the fallout from Galliano's antisemitic tirade, stating in press announcements that it would "address the derogatory conduct that fundamentally altered his career and public reception". "In doing so, the exhibition will consider how artistic achievement should be understood alongside ethical accountability."

stories.title: Galway university 'fake news' expert claims fake doctorate
stories.summary: A leading Irish academic and former Fulbright scholar who is an expert on disinformation and 'fake news' has been falsely claiming to have a doctorate from a distinguished English university, Prime Time has established. Tom Felle, an associate professor at University of Galway's Department of Journalism and Media who was head of the department until last year, has been described as "Dr Tom Felle" on the university’s website, including in prospectuses designed to attract students to study at the college. In a submission on University of Galway branded notepaper earlier this year to the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport, he was also presented as "Dr Tom Felle". Mr Felle claims to have a doctorate in journalism from City, University of London (now City St George’s), where he used to work as a senior lecturer. The university’s department of journalism is widely regarded as the most prestigious of its type in Britain. A former senior academic at City St George's told Prime Time that "Tom registered for a PhD by prior publication with a City supervisor. However, the degree was not completed and he left the university a couple of years afterwards and did not pursue the PhD. He was therefore never awarded the degree." Mr Felle, a former journalist, has appeared on television and radio and in print as an expert on media issues, especially disinformation and online abuse of female politicians. In 2024, he was appointed as an expert assessor for the media regulator Coimisiún na Meán.

stories.title: IAG sees 2026 capacity slightly down year-on-year
stories.summary: Aer Lingus and British Airways owner IAG has today forecast its annual capacity would be slightly lower than a year earlier, as flight disruptions in the Middle East stemming from the ongoing Iran war and other regional conflicts weighed on operations. The airline's third-quarter operating profit before exceptional items of €1.73 billion also missed analysts' consensus of €1.81 billion, as the global aviation sector struggles with rising fuel costs stemming from the war. However, IAG said 85% of expected forward bookings for the fourth quarter were secured, with numbers for the first quarter of 2027 looking strong. Its total fuel cost is expected to be €8.9 billion for the year, with IAG being currently 45% hedged against volatilities for 2027.

stories.title: Elding's U21 redeployment 'certainly not a step down'
stories.summary: The decision to call Owen Elding into the Republic of Ireland under-21s squad instead of the senior set-up should not be viewed as a "step down", according to Jim Crawford, as the opportunity to make history beckons this month. The Boys in Green under-21 head coach is preparing for a crucial European Championship play-off against Finland. The first leg will come next Friday, 13 November in Tampere, before the second leg in Cork the following Tuesday. stories.title: Resdiscovering Eithne Strong - The Lyric Feature goes deep
stories.summary: In this Sunday's Lyric Feature, presenter and producer Joanna Marsden goes In the Deeps as she unfolds the life of West Limerick writer Eithne Strong (1923–1999), who broke with her repressive Catholic upbringing to live an unconventional life amidst Ireland’s first Freudian psychoanalytic circle. I walk a lot – mainly close to my home – and when I walk, I often think about the streets and buildings I pass, and the people who walked here before me, especially those not long gone and still held in the memories of the living. I’m always listening for the names of these people, who seem to reside in a liminal zone between now and the past, where, if we pay attention, there is just enough time to catch their stories before they disappear. In the Deeps originated when I heard in passing that the psychoanalytic movement in Ireland had begun in a house in Monkstown, Co Dublin, not far from Dun Laoghaire, where I live. This led me to a paper by historian Fergus Campbell, which included a photo of the home of Ireland’s first Freudian psychoanalyst, Jonathan Hanaghan. It was a house I recognised from my walks. The paper described the group of analysts trained by Hanaghan in the 1940s, including Englishman Rupert Strong. There was a photo of Rupert with his young wife Eithne and their first child, Jennifer. Eithne was described as a writer but though I studied Irish Writing at Trinity College, I’d never come across her name. I held the image of Eithne’s face – the pale eyes that seemed to be elsewhere – in the back of my mind for a few months while I followed various trails. I visited Rosalind Matthews, the engaging 96-year-old daughter of Jonathan Hanaghan. I walked by Rosalind’s childhood home so often that I noticed the current owners’ habit of turning on an old-fashioned standard lamp at dusk, illuminating Hanaghan’s former consulting room. I explored housing estates on the edge of Monkstown and Dun Laoghaire, trying to locate the former site of the psychoanalytic commune that Hanaghan established in 1948. Then, knowing more of the world Eithne Strong (née O’Connell) had married into, I came back to her. Her books were out of print, but the reading room in the Lexicon Library had a copy of Flesh… The Greatest Sin, her book-length narrative poem about her West Limerick upbringing, published in 1980. Five minutes after I opened Flesh, I knew I wanted to make a documentary about Eithne. The characters in the poem felt like bruised, caged creatures, imprisoned by the society in which they lived. But they also felt modern and alive, their individual energies pulsing beneath the surface, finding relief not in a religious God but in nature.

stories.title: Comedian Frank Carson to be honoured in Belfast
stories.summary: Belfast comedian Frank Carson is set to be honoured with a blue plaque in his memory at his former school in the city. Carson, who appeared on TV series Opportunity Knocks and Tiswas, was perhaps best known for his trademark quips, "It's the way I tell them" and "It’s a cracker". Carson, who also twice served as mayor of Balbriggan, Co Dublin, died at aged 85 in 2012 at his home in Blackpool, Lancashire following an illness. Crowds turned out for his funeral in Belfast where they heard Carson described as the "prime minister of fun". Now his memory is being made permanent at St Patrick’s National School in Belfast where an Ulster History Circle blue plaque will be erected. "For the Carson family, this blue plaque brings dad back home, fixing his legacy where Hugh Francis Carson’s story began," he said.

stories.title: 36% of adults who suffer abuse take no action - survey
stories.summary: More than one third of people who believe they are experiencing adult abuse take no action, according to Safeguarding Ireland. A REDC survey of 1,000 adults found that more than one third (36%) did not act in circumstances where they believed that abuse was happening to them. Some 20% said they did nothing because they did not know what to do, while 16% said they chose not to act. When compared with previous REDC surveys, Safeguarding Ireland found there was "a significant increase" in online abuse. It was identified by 40% of respondents, with the same figure for psychological abuse. Coercive control was experienced by 32% Adult abuse appears to be "widespread", according to Safeguarding Ireland, with almost two thirds (63%) saying that they had either personally experienced or witnessed abuse of another person.

stories.title: Airbnb lifts annual revenue growth forecast
stories.summary: Airbnb has raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast, as the holiday rental platform bets on resilient global leisure travel demand, sending its shares up 11% in extended trading on Wall Street. Travel firms are banking on steady demand for international travel, buoyed by corporate travel and spending by affluent customers despite inflation and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. The San Francisco-based company now expects annual revenue growth in the "high teens," compared with its "at least mid-teens" forecast earlier. The company also authorised a new repurchase programme of up to an additional $12 billion of Airbnb's Class A common stock. Globally, nights and seats booked, a metric that includes both room stays and service bookings, rose 16% to 155 million in the third quarter. Quarterly bookings in North America grew by "low double digit" year over year, and in the "mid-teens" in EMEA.

stories.title: Decent innings for Byrne, Foster and Walsh in Asia
stories.summary: It was a mixed Friday for the Irish on the Ladies European Tour and LPGA Tour events in Asia. Sara Byrne and Anna Foster are in a tie for 30th place after day two of the Aramco China Championship on the LET Tour. Byrne, who opened with a round of one-under-par, 72, made four birdies and one bogey on Friday for a round of three-under-par, 70. Birdies at two, three and seven were interwoven with her only bogey of the day on the fourth hole to go out in 34 hots. Another birdie followed at the par-five 11th hole to move up the leaderboard. Foster started her round one shot better off than Byrne, also birdied the 11th as her second hole of the day, before picking up another shot on the 16th to make the turn in two-under. Another birdie followed on the second, her 11th hole, before a bogey on four led to a second round score of two-under-par, 71, for the second day running.

stories.title: The secret history of female jazz bands in the Irish Free State
stories.summary: Analysis: The explosion of jazz in the 1920s and 1930s is a reminder that Irish cultural life then was richer and more complex than we often assume A news report in the Evening Herald in December 1926 reported two 17 year old girls had "disappeared" from their home in Clonmel. The pair, Winifred Long and her maid Annie Brown, were believed to be in London seeking work in a nightclub as jazz singers and percussionists. Winifred's father was the editor of the Clonmel Nationalist newspaper who drew on his network of newspaper contacts to track down his daughter. A few weeks later, the Yorkshire Post Intelligencer reported the young women had been found working in Woolworth's in Bradford, their dreams of stardom not quite realised. The case of the runaway teens highlights the popularity of jazz music and its accompanying dance crazes all across Ireland during the 1920s. It was a time of greater freedom, especially for women, in social mobility and career prospects. Their buying power could be seen in the fashion for shorter hair and looser clothing. Jazz was, at its heart, a dance culture, and the style known as "hot jazz" was music made for dancing; energetic, syncopated and full of the same high spirits that drove the Charleston craze of the 1920s, here just as everywhere else. From British Pathé, dancers with the Covent Garden Band bust some moves Researcher Sean Shanagher suggests we have an 'historical amnesia’ about the popularity of jazz dancing in Ireland, choosing instead to think of live music from this period as traditional and ceilidh bands. Instead, his research shows 80% of adverts in the Roscommon Herald in 1930 were for modern dance bands. The explosion of jazz as a popular form sparked a powerful and organised backlash from conservative voices, although in truth this was often long after jazz dance bands were established events on the social circuit. The craze for "hot jazz" was supercharged from 1924 when the BBC relayed live dance music from the Savoy Hotel in London. Anybody with a half decent radio set could pick up broadcasts from high power transmitters in Britain, and under the right conditions, from the continent. When 2RN started broadcasting in 1926, its programming finished at 10.30pm, just in time to pick up the dance broadcasts from the Savoy.

stories.title: Nearly 90m displaced facing severe climate risks - UN
stories.summary: Three-quarters of the world's displaced people live in countries facing severe exposure to climate-related hazards, the United Nations said, calling for urgent action to protect them. Days before the COP31 climate conference starts in Turkey, a UN refugee agency report said nearly 90 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people faced severe risks linked to a warming planet. "Refugees face a double injustice," said Anton Leis Garcia, UNHCR's assistant high commissioner for operations. "Forced to flee conflicts they did not cause, they are now on the frontlines of a climate crisis they have contributed least to." People forced to flee conflict, violence and persecution find themselves in places grappling with severe droughts, deadly floods and extreme heat, the organisation pointed out. Climate change was also increasingly threatening the prospect of lasting solutions for displaced people, UNHCR said.

stories.title: NFL: Jaguars dismantle Ravens in dominant win
stories.summary: Trevor Lawrence passed for 242 yards and one touchdown and Cam Little kicked four field goals as the Jacksonville Jaguars sailed to a 33-10 victory over the host Baltimore Ravens on a rainy Thursday night. Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. rushed for touchdowns and Parker Washington had ‌a scoring reception for the Jaguars (6-2), who won for the fifth time in the past six games. Montaric Brown and Jourdan Lewis had interceptions and Jalen McLeod recovered a fumble as Jacksonville held the Ravens to 227 total yards. Lawrence completed 16 of 26 passes. Baltimore (4-5) lost its fourth consecutive game and was unable to mount a passing attack due to long-term injuries to Lamar Jackson (right thumb) and Tyler Huntley (right toe). ⁠Both players were hurt on Sunday in a loss to the Buffalo Bills. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano made his first career NFL start and completed 10 of 18 passes for 60 yards and two interceptions. Justice Hill raced 65 yards on a fourth-quarter run for Baltimore's lone touchdown. Derrick Henry rushed for 57 yards on 17 carries and moved into seventh place on the NFL's all-time rushing list with 13,707 yards. He passed Jerome Bettis (13,662) and LaDainian Tomlinson (13,684). In sixth place is Curtis Martin (14,101).

stories.title: Preview: Time is now for Ireland to begin RWC push
stories.summary: If there's a silver lining in what's been an up and down couple of years for this Irish team, it's that we haven't had to worry that they've peaked too soon. Andy Farrell and his fellow coaches aren't in denial about where this side currently are in the food chain. Asked on Wednesday where they need to improve between now and the World Cup in Australia next year, the head coach's answer of "every area" was, in his own words, the "obvious and boring" answer. By his own admission, the team couldn't go to a World Cup tomorrow morning with the 100% belief that they could win it, an honest assessment which speaks to the ground that has to be made on South Africa, France and New Zealand. As other teams have shown in the past, there is plenty of time to turn things around, but without signs of clear progress this month, that timeline becomes tense. With so much of the focus this week on where Ireland need to get better, very little media focus has been put on this week's opponents.

stories.title: Porter ready to play 'smarter, not harder' at the scrum
stories.summary: It's almost been a year since Andrew Porter's last taste of Test rugby, and it left a sour note. The loosehead prop was one of five Irish players carded in last November's bonkers 24-13 defeat to South Africa at Aviva Stadium, a day when Ireland's scrum was obliterated by the Boks. Since then, Porter has had to deal with two calf injuries which landed at the worst possible time. The first, in January of this year, ruled him out for the Six Nations, while another late in the URC season cost him a place on Ireland's summer tour. With a full pre-season and four outings for Leinster under his belt, the 30-year-old is fighting fit and back in Andy Farrell's side for this evening's Nations Championship clash with Argentina at Aviva Stadium. For Farrell, this window is about starting the catch-up process on New Zealand, France and South Africa. For Porter, it's about catching up on a year out of Test rugby. "There's a few minor things [that have changed], but as a whole, it's the same kind of messages from the coaches," he says.

stories.title: Cancer trials saved State €6.5m in drug costs - charity
stories.summary: The State has saved €6.51 million in drug costs based on a sample of 38 cancer clinical trials which took place in the last 12 months, Cancer Trials Ireland has said. The trials included 230 people between September 2025 and August of this year. Cancer Trials Ireland said that, when a patient enrols on a clinical trial, their treatment costs - such as medicines, imaging, blood and other tests, as well as biopsies and procedures - are generally paid for by the sponsor. Where this happens, there is no cost to the patient, their health insurer, or the State. The charity’s 'Value of Cancer Trials 2’ report estimates total savings, investments and revenue to the State of €23.77m over 12 months. In addition to the €6.51m in drug cost savings, the report estimates that 20 trials resulted in inward investment of €6.76m by pharmaceutical companies, relating to experimental medicines.

No one knows more than the boss that Ireland are not exactly where they need to be ahead of a World Cup year.

stories.title: Cup final excitement reaches fever pitch in Derry
stories.summary: The anticipation in Derry ahead of Sunday's FAI Cup Final at the Aviva Stadium has brought excitement, joy and pride to a new generation of football fans in the northwest. Ahead of the final against Waterford FC, the Candystripes have visited schools across Derry, including Ardnashee School and College, one of Northern Ireland's largest special schools. In a scene of unbridled enthusiasm and happiness this week, students delivered a rousing rendition of the Derry anthem Teenage Kicks for the team and management. Ardnashee's Director of Post-16, Darren Gibson, said it was fabulous for their students to meet their Derry City heroes, noting that many will make the journey to Dublin. "I think about 90% of the school support the team, and the other 10% are going to support them after today," he said. "It's absolutely fabulous for them. "It's special times and it's going to be some game," student Ryan Clements said, as the team heads into their third FAI Cup final in five seasons.

stories.title: COP31 summit faces tough test as climate threats mount
stories.summary: Nearly 200 nations will gather for the COP31 summit in Turkey on Monday but tensions over geopolitics, finance and fossil fuels are tempering expectations of a major breakthrough in tackling the climate crisis. More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN's two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya that run from 9 to 20 November. Tougher action on fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, appears unlikely and budget-strapped developed countries are reluctant to commit more money to help developing nations cope with climate impacts. An energy crisis and cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the war in the Middle East, are also looming over the gathering. "This is not going to be the COP that changes the world," said Paul Watkinson, France's former chief negotiator at climate summits. "It's an intermediate COP in many ways. But it is an important conference and it does need to make sure it makes progress," he said.

stories.title: Newsom to commute death sentences for 548 on death row
stories.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom has said he will commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates currently condemned to execution in his state, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere. The announcement, in a three-page letter addressed to "all Californians," came as Mr Newsom, a Democrat who is expected to seek his party's presidential nomination in 2028, neared the end of his second and final four-year term as governor. "I have decided to exercise my constitutional clemency authority to commute all California death sentences to life without the possibility of parole," he wrote. Mr Newsom, who previously served as mayor of San Francisco and lieutenant governor, declared a moratorium on executions in March 2019, about two months after first taking office as governor. California last put a prisoner to death in 2006 when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Mr Newsom wrote in his announcement.

stories.title: Passenger recalls 'terrifying' alert on Aer Lingus flight
stories.summary: A passenger on an Aer Lingus flight, which was diverted due to a security threat this morning, has described seeing French air force jets escort the plane to an air field in France. Aer Lingus Flight EI402 left Dublin Airport at 6.24am this morning, travelling to Rome Fiumicino Airport. What had started off as a trip to Rome for a friend's wedding ended up with an unexpected stopover in France. Katie McAteer from Dublin and her five friends boarded their Aer Lingus flight to Rome this morning looking forward to the next few days, which would see them celebrating their friend's wedding in the Italian capital. But around an hour and 15 minutes into the flight the pilot announced a problem with the plane and that they would have to land in Paris. Ms McAteer said they were aware of security alerts on flights over the past couple of days, so that immediately came to her mind.

stories.title: LIV Golf to be liquidated as financing deal collapses
stories.summary: LIV Golf has announced it intends to "transition to an orderly wind-down of its operations", bringing an end to the controversial breakaway tour. The Financial Times reported BC Partners Credit, who had been lined up as potential backers following the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, had pulled out of a deal worth more than £200 million due to an exodus of star players. LIV, which launched in 2022, was forced to apply for chapter 11 bankruptcy, effectively cancelling playing contracts, with the likes of Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton, Louis Oosthuizen and Lee Westwood departing. A statement from LIV on Thursday read: "LIV Golf Incorporated and its affiliates today announced that it intends to transition to an orderly wind-down of its operations. "Since April 2026, the League’s leadership team, with the support of its independent directors and advisors, has run a disciplined and thorough process to identify the best, value-maximising path forward for the company and its stakeholders. "That process produced a proposed recapitalisation transaction contemplated by the company’s Restructuring Support Agreement with BC Partners Advisors, the credit business of BC Partners, which the company sought to implement through its voluntary chapter 11 proceedings in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey.

stories.title: Aer Lingus plane among 27 flights hit by bomb hoaxes
stories.summary: Hoax bomb threats affected at least 27 flights around Europe today from Ireland to Bulgaria, forcing some to make unplanned landings and prompting fighter jets to escort or intercept others. While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come as many European officials are accusing Russia of masterminding sabotage and 'hybrid attacks' - which are often cheap, easily deniable and not expected to trigger an armed response. Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by today's disruptions, have previously accused Moscow directly, while Germany blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport in August. Britain has blamed Russia in the past but linked Iran to a suspected plot to attack a US air base recently. Both Russia and Iran deny any involvement. An Aer Lingus flight which left Dublin Airport at 6.24am this morning, travelling to Rome Fiumicino Airport, was diverted as a "security precaution". French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office said fighter jets were sent to intercept and escort the Aer Lingus Flight EI402 after the pilot did not cooperate with authorities as expected.
